blocks.x: Harlan Coben is one of the most influential contemporary thriller writers working today. His novels Fool Me Once, Run Away, and Stay Close have all been adapted into Netflix originals. I Will Find You, his most recent record-breaking adaptation starring Sam Worthington and Britt Lower, is now in the top ten most-watched English Netflix shows of all time. With such a consistent track record of crime drama hits, a Harlan Coben endorsement certainly carries some weight.

Among Coben’s thriller book recommendations is The Collective. Published in 2021 by Edgar Award-winning author Alison Gaylin, this psychological thriller is about a group of mothers brought together for some vigilante justice. Coben called The Collective “her best book yet,” with “a knockout of an ending.” Before its publication five years ago, Yellow Bird UK optioned the rights to Gaylin’s book to develop it into a TV series, but no further confirmations or updates on the adaptation have been released since then.
'The Collective' Is an Enthralling Dark Web Thriller

blocks.c: The Collective by Alison Gaylin book cover.

blocks.x: The protagonist of The Collective is Camille Gardener, a grieving mother whose teenage daughter, Emily, died at a fraternity party five years ago. Camille is completely unmoored, not just in grief but in overwhelming rage that Emily’s accused killer, Harris Blanchard, essentially walked free. No consequences and no backlash. When Camille learns that Harris is receiving a humanitarian award at his university, she has a breakdown and crashes the event. This public display, which is swiftly recorded and shared all over social media, kicks off chapter one and brings Camille into the sights of a covert group of mothers who want revenge for their dead children.

Prompted by a very ominous, sparse business card, Camille quickly goes down the digital rabbit hole and eventually ends up in an anonymous dark web chatroom site for women looking to take justice into their own hands. At first, Camille assumes the chat is purely for venting or role-playing revenge fantasies. However, Camille finds much more than a space of shared commiseration about a failed justice system. This underground alliance offers an actionable alternative, but once you're in the collective, it's hard to get out. Usually, the dark web is used conceptually for straight-up internet horror, but Gaylin's approach, grounded in the dark side of grief, results in a popcorn thriller that shakes a straightforward understanding of accountability and villainy.
Who doesn’t love watching someone finally get their sweet, sweet, revenge?
This Isn’t Your Typical “Good for Her” Revenge Story

blocks.c: Carey Mulligan and Alfred Molina talking in Promising Young Woman (2020).

blocks.x: Vigilante justice is definitely a slippery slope, and Alison Gaylin's novel is not interested in sketching revenge as satisfying and uncomplicated. The female revenge or "good for her" movie is a popular subgenre in the thriller and horror space that tends to deliver more clear-cut, entertaining revenge arcs. Some memorable cinematic examples include Uma Thurman in Kill Bill, Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl, the various remakes of Stephen King's Carrie, Jennifer Garner in Peppermint, and more recently, Carey Mulligan in Promising Young Woman. The latter is perhaps the closest to Gaylin's contribution to the genre in that it doesn't tie up the story with a happy ending.

The tragic, all-consuming undercurrent of The Collective is foreshadowed by the name of the mother-made group: Niobe. A symbol of eternal maternal grief in Greek Mythology, Niobe loses her children as punishment for her hubris in mocking the female Titan, Leto. Her fate? Well, Niobe fled to Mount Sipylus, where the gods turned her into a weeping stone. This brutal mythology involving two female figures immediately signals a different layer of conflict in the story, concerned not with a female vigilante against a male perpetrator, but with another vengeful violence happening between women.

What ultimately makes Gaylin's novel such a standout thriller is that catharsis is not its object. Although the story invokes the "strength and power of collective rage," it, too, shows the danger in said rage. An increasingly timely read due to its spotlight on today's digital-era vigilantism, The Collective is a book about anonymity, desperation, and the gift/burden of being seen. Coben's high marks for this dark thriller's twisty plot, pulling readers into the abyss, are well-earned and point to this story's potential for a screen adaptation.
